messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Understanding bad performance
parts:
I  have a model that I'm having performance problems with -- a single update takes over 10 seconds, N_Eff is much less than 1/10 of the posterior sample size, and the tree depth after warmup averages 8 or 9. This model has over 8000 variables restricted to lie between 0 and 1. I thought that maybe the problem is due to variable values near the constraint boundaries. No single one of the variables has a mean closer than about 0.085 to one of the boundaries. However, with over 8000 variables, there tends to be at least one variable that is very close to a constraint boundary on any given time step. If I take the minimum (over all 8000+ variables) of the distance to a constraint boundary at every time step, the mean of this minimum over all time steps is about 6e-5.

My impression is that even a single variable very close to a constraint boundary can cause problems. Is this correct? This suggests that my problem is simply that I have 8000+ interval-constrained variables that can plausibly vary over the entire interval; that is, I'm going to run into performance problems with ANY model that has such a large number of interval-constrained variables whose values can plausibly range over the entire interval. Is my thinking here correct?

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Understanding bad performance
parts:
This is just a manifestation of concentration of measure — as the number of dimensions
increases the probability mass on a hypercube concentrates at the corners, and this
tends to overwhelm the posterior unless there is a tremendous amount of data.

Provided that you’re declaring your parameters as constrained between 0 and 1 then
there’s nothing inherently bad about approaching the boundaries.  On the unconstrained
scale the is exponentially more “room” near the boundaries so sampling should be okay,
if a bit slower.

What exactly is the N_eff / N ratio?  Does your model have hierarchical structure?  Is there
prior information you can impose to help constrain the values?  Honestly its just sounds like 
you have a really, really big model with not a lot of information from the data/priors.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Understanding bad performance
parts:
I'd like to emphasise Michael's point that if the variables are constrained in the definition, then in a sense the boundaries are not boundaries at all. (Is it even possible to set up priors that make the sampler diverging on the unconstrained scale?)

In general, it is not always easy to find out why sampling is slow. Seemingly minor details in priors or in the model may make a big difference. Sometimes adding parameters to the model to make it fit the data better makes sampling faster. 

A good approach is to start with a small subset of data, if possible, to try out different parameterisations and priors. 

(I have a model fit currently in rstan that has over 32,000 parameters, with about 300,000 samples. I managed to generate 100 samples in 6 hours, and n_eff is good enough for my purposes.)

On Thursday, February 27, 2014 1:49:55 PM UTC+2, Michael Betancourt wrote:

(I have a model fit currently in rstan that has over 32,000 parameters, with about 300,000 samples. I managed to generate 100 samples in 6 hours, and n_eff is good enough for my purposes.)
 
Wow, that's incredible!  Can you share some details of the model?  We're always looking for more success stories as they tend to be under-reported around these parts.  :-)

I could share the whole model, but it's not too entertaining, just a large sparse logistic linear "mixture model" with hierarchy, normal priors for parameters, etc. The model could be fitted with lme4, but initial tests did not look promising (convergence problems, I did not test lme4 thoroughly), so ended up using Stan. This is a toy project, so far at least. I estimated the abundance changes of Finnish butterflies from open data and tried to compensate for variation in observational intensity: https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/8403120/rhop.png. Most of the parameters are about abundance at locations, per species. Maybe they could be marginalised away.

As expected and already known, there is a southern invasion going on. If I manage to write a blog entry of the results, I'll share it here. 

More professionally, I work in a "data scientist" consultant team, and we have played with Stan a lot and even used it in a couple of projects. Our problems often seem to be at the edge of scalability of current Stan and HMC, so we're impatiently waiting for posterior approximation techniques. :) That is, the problems are not really "big data" projects, but often too big to be conveniently estimated with Stan/HMC.  Still there is often enough structure making straightforward use of standard tools impossible or suboptimal. Stan and probabilistic programming in general have a huge potential in this niche, IMO.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Understanding bad performance
parts:
Here are some stats for the latest run on this model.

For lp__, N_Eff / N = 0.0019.

 Of the 13,886 parameters,

* 75.6% (10,492) have N_Eff / N = 1

* 24.2% (3,355) have N_Eff / N in the range [0.1, 1)

* 0.27% (38) have N_Eff / N in the range [0.01, 0.1)

* One has N_Eff / N == 0.0039.

treedepth__ is usually 9 after warmup. During warmup it usually ranges between 8 and 11.

The three chains took 15.8, 21.7, and 12.9 seconds per iteration during warmup. They took 11.1, 10.2, and 6.2 seconds per iteration during sampling.

This is a multinomial probit model with a full covariance matrix, used for analyzing survey data. Each of the survey responses is Likert scale (ordinal), and has a corresponding continuous latent variable. The observed responses are derived from the latent responses via a vector of cutpoints, plus two individual-level scale-usage parameters that scale and translate the cutpoint vector. The scale-usage parameters have a hierarchical structure.

The constraints are the data: each latent response must lie between an upper and lower bound determined by the ordinal response. This is actually implemented by having parameters constrained to lie between 0 and 1, and then obtaining the latent responses as transformed parameters by scaling and translating.
